title: Value units and discounting guidelines — token framing & tier guidance
content:
TL;DR
We should double-down on tokens as the core unit of value for Redwood’s hosted API and self-serve tiers because tokens: (1) map directly to cost drivers (compute + memory), (2) give fine-grained visibility to customers, and (3) support heterogeneous workloads (generation, embeddings, reranking). For enterprise/Dedicated, expose equivalent metrics (rps, reserved throughput, seats for admin controls) but keep the customer-facing language tied to tokens/credits so incentives align.

Objectives for this doc
- Provide a clear internal rationale for token pricing that PM, sales, and docs can reference.
- Recommend a pragmatic tier structure and discounting primitives that work for self-serve and sales-assisted deals.
- Give short sales scripts for common objections and competitive differentiation bullets.

1) Metric framing: what we measure and why
Guiding principle: bill for the dominant marginal cost drivers and make unit semantics simple for developers. For LLM inference those are primarily: input tokens + output tokens (attn/KV work scales with seq length) and model choice.
- Unit: token (input + output) aggregated daily/monthly.
- Why tokens vs requests/messages/characters/MB: tokens correlate with GPU time and memory usage better than request count or characters. A single request could be 2 tokens or 2k tokens — token pricing exposes this.
- Secondary metrics surfaced but not billed: requests/second (useful for SLOs), peak concurrency, embedding-vector-ops (for embedding-heavy customers we may surface per-embedding pricing as token-equivalent).
- Price multipliers by model class (small/medium/large/quantized): same token -> different $ depending on model family. Keep multiplier names simple: base, pro, high-capacity.

2) Why token pricing (short internal pitch)
- Aligns incentives: customers paying by tokens are incentivized to optimize prompts and use caching/batching — which improves economics for both Redwood and the customer.
- Predictability at scale: tokens enable simple conversion between usage patterns and spend forecasts (easier for finance and customers than per-request).
- Granularity and fairness: token unit handles bursty and long-sequence use cases fairly.
- Operational mapping: tokens map to scheduling/packing heuristics in the runtime, so accounting ties to real resource allocation.

3) Alternatives and tradeoffs (what we considered)
- Per-request pricing: simpler headline, but can misprice long sequences and disincentivize legitimate heavy usage. Bad signals for embeddings and batch inference.
- Seat-based (per-seat): works for Dashboard/Console administration, but not for inference consumption. Use seats as an add-on for admin controls and SSO/UAM.
- Throughput/Reservation billing: reserved-GPU capacity is ideal for Dedicated products. Keep it as separate SKU (monthly commit) rather than the core token metric.

4) Tier structure (recommended — names and intent)
- Developer (free/low-cost entry): small monthly token allotment + pay-as-you-go overage. Aimed at quick experimentation and PLG funnel.
  - Example: 200k free tokens, then $X / 1M tokens on base models. Onboarding flow: sign-up, show tokens remaining, suggestion cards to enable batching and KV caching.
- Team (self-serve paid): predictable monthly credit package, developer collaboration features, usage dashboards. Volume discounts start here via bundled credits.
- Scale (sales-assisted): committed monthly credits at a discount (commitment-based bands), advanced routing controls, and higher concurrency limits.
- Enterprise / Dedicated: contract with reserved capacity, SLA, private deployment pricing. Token accounting still used internally for chargeback and showback.

Important tier mechanics
- Model multipliers: tiers charge per-token base rate * model multiplier. Make multipliers explicit in billing UI ("gpt-x: 1.8x base").
- Credit expiry: avoid very short expiry. Recommend 12-month expiry for pre-purchased credits for self-serve, negotiable for enterprise.
- Overage behavior: soft throttle + overage billing at list rate; for committed accounts bill overages monthly.

5) Discounting language and primitives (how sales should talk about discounts)
- Core levers: term length, committed monthly spend, model-selection guarantee, telemetry/integration fee bundle.
- Discount rules (guideline):
  - 10–20%: small annual commitments (~$X–$Y/month range) — enable for self-serve-to-sales conversions.
  - 20–35%: mid-level commitments (12-month, multi-region). Includes prioritized onboarding and a small reserved pool.
  - 35%+: large deals only, tied to multi-year commitments, minimum consumption floors, and/or dedicated capacity purchases. These should require RevOps/Finance sign-off.
- Anchor discounts to committed effective price ("you commit to $Z/month and get 25% off list token rate") instead of item-level ad-hoc discounts. This keeps math simple and predictable.
- Usage protections: establish an annual true-up (so customers aren’t penalized for accidental under-commit) and an overage cap if desired as a negotiation tool.
- Language for offers (sales microcopy):
  - "With a 12‑month commitment, we can offer a 25% discount to your effective token rate and guarantee your access to reserved capacity during peak windows."
  - "We can structure a pilot credit package with a capped overage so you can test at scale without surprise bills."

6) UI microcopy and billing UX suggestions (self-serve)
- Billing page: show 'tokens used this month', equivalent API calls, and an "Estimate this month" projection based on trailing 7/30d usage.
- When switching models: show delta preview: "Switching to model X will increase per-token cost by 2.0x — estimated monthly cost change: +$YYY".
- Purchase flow: "Buy credits" modal with clear expiry, effective per-token price at the selected quantity, and a checkbox for auto-renew commitment.

7) Competitive notes & positioning bullets (how to win the convo)
- Against plug-and-play APIs (simplicity-first): emphasize transparent per-token economics, operational tooling (rollouts, tracing), and tooling that reduces unit cost (auto-caching, batching).
- Against cloud provider endpoints: emphasize Redwood’s model catalog and optimized runtime (lower effective $/token via better batching/quantization) + simpler cross-region routing + predictable SLAs.
- Against open-source/self-hosted vendors: highlight managed fallback policies, zero-oncall requirement, and integrated cost-optimization features.

8) Objections and sales scripts (short)
- Objection: "We prefer per-request pricing — tokens are confusing."
  - Script: "I get that. Tokens map directly to compute and sequence length — the benefit is transparency: you’ll see the exact resource cost signal and can immediately reduce spend with caching/shorter prompts. We also show estimated cost per call in the console so you can make decisions at the request level."
- Objection: "What if our app has variable long contexts?"
  - Script: "We recommend keeping a cache/prefix strategy for long static context and only send deltas. For predictable heavy workloads we also offer reserved capacity with a token-based showback model so you never get surprise throttling."

9) Rollout plan & open questions (for PMs and RevOps)
- Rollout phases:
  1) Internal alignment doc (this one) + finance modeling of revenue under token vs hybrid metrics (2 weeks).
  2) Self-serve UI changes: token visibility, model multiplier display, credit purchase (4–6 weeks).
  3) Sales enablement kit: objection scripts, discount framework, sample term sheets (2 weeks).
  4) Pilot offers for 3–5 customers to validate discount bands and expiry behavior (quarter-long pilots).
- Open questions / TODOs:
  - Decide default credit expiry window (recommend 12 months; finalize with Finance).
  - Define thresholds for automatic RevOps review (>35% discount or >$X committed monthly).
  - Confirm exact model multipliers and map to SKU names (action: applied-ml to propose multipliers).

Appendix: quick pricing examples (illustrative only)
- Base list: $0.40 / 1M tokens on base model (example).
- Model multiplier: medium = 1.5x, large = 3.0x.
- Developer tier: first 200k tokens free, then PAYG at list.
- Scale pilot: commit $25k/month for 12 months = 20% discount on list, plus reserved concurrency pool.

Notes to self / signoffs needed
- Final signoff from Finance and Legal on credit expiry and refund rules.
- Product to wire up per-model multiplier visibility in billing UI.
- Sales ops to add discounting thresholds to the quoting tool.

References & links
- See attached confluence doc for modeling sheets (confluence:PRICING-2025-token-framework).
- Related tickets: jira:GTMPOL-342 (discount bands), github:pr/1123 (billing UI prototype).

End of doc — comments welcome.
